claims.claim: The United States has a federal court system and separate state court systems; state systems vary in their intermediate and highest courts.
The federal structure includes 94 district courts, 13 courts of appeals below the Supreme Court, and specialized federal courts or tribunals; the simplified three-tier picture is not exhaustive.
Federal district courts serve as trial courts that determine facts and apply law, while courts of appeals review whether law was applied correctly in a trial court or federal administrative agency.
Subject-matter jurisdiction concerns the issues or category of case, and personal jurisdiction concerns authority over the parties; they are distinct high-level jurisdictional concepts.

In the federal system, decisions of higher courts bind lower courts on applicable questions, while a decision from another circuit may be persuasive rather than binding; precedent must be evaluated in context.

State courts ordinarily give the final word on state-law questions, subject to U.S. Supreme Court review of qualifying federal questions, and state court names or structures cannot be assumed to be uniform.
A court-system overview cannot identify the correct forum or predict a real business dispute because outcomes depend on current law, jurisdiction, procedural requirements, and facts.
